title: Clavicular and the Business of Contempt
dek: He sold boys a new face and a theory of women. Now Braden Peters is charged with rape in Massachusetts. He says he did nothing wrong. Here's the file.
body: The charges were filed in Massachusetts in September. Braden Peters, 20, the livestreamer who calls himself Clavicular, is accused of rape, of drugging a person for sexual intercourse, and of buying alcohol for someone under 21. The person was a 17-year-old girl. The date was May 2025. The place was his family's house on Cape Cod.
Peters denies all of it. Nothing has been proven. A courtroom will decide this, not a comment section.

According to the police narrative NPR described, the girl had been talking with Peters about appearing on his streams. She told police he instructed her to say she was 18 on camera and to call the vodka water. She said she got drunk and that the sex that followed was not consensual. The Associated Press reported her account that she woke the next morning to Peters raping her.

His answer went up on social media. He posted what he presented as a thank-you note and a video involving her, and wrote, in a post Us Weekly reported, "Happens to all successful young men." His framing: she's after money. His lawyer denies the allegations and disputes her account.

In October she dropped the sexual-assault claims from a separate civil suit in Florida. Her attorney told NBC News she did it so the civil case wouldn't get in the way of the Massachusetts prosecution. The criminal charges stand. An Oct. 14 arraignment was canceled. The docket shows the next hearing on Oct. 22.
That's where things are. Here's how he got here.
## The boy and the forum

Peters grew up in Hoboken, New Jersey. He told The New York Times he struggled socially at school and ordered testosterone online shortly before he turned 15. When his parents threw out his supply, he had the next shipments sent to a post office box. He fell into Looksmax.org, the forum where young men grade each other's faces and trade methods for changing their own. He later said Sacred Heart University expelled him after steroids turned up in his dorm.

The trouble started early. In the summer of 2024 he was arrested after a bar fight; the assault-and-battery charges were later dismissed, Variety reported. That December he crashed a car. On the forum, he blamed falling asleep after taking baclofen, a muscle relaxant. The officer's report, Miami New Times found, noted wet, icy roads.
## The breakout

In October 2025 he went on another streamer's broadcast, Cheesur's, to talk about his hair loss, and the forum kid found a real audience. A month later, in an interview with Jack Neel that KTAR later dug up, he said: "I'm pretty much using meth for hollow cheeks."

By February the Times reported he was pulling in more than $100,000 a month on Kick. He streamed dates with female fans and explained why people watched: "People watch them because they can't get girls." On an outing with a woman who shared his interest in looksmaxxing, he told her, "It's a male space." He told the paper he believed testosterone had left him infertile.

GQ followed him through New York that month, where he walked for designer Elena Velez. He called Sydney Sweeney "malformed," said women shouldn't be allowed to vote, and claimed he had hit his own face with a hammer to reshape the bones, a practice the forum calls bonesmashing.
## The academy

For a fee, Peters sold an online course. A reporter paid $49 to get in for Rolling Stone and came out describing extreme bodily self-punishment paired with instructions that, in his words, normalized sexual coercion. The Guardian quoted one line from it: "inch closer until your erection is her problem."
Read that one twice. It's the whole philosophy in seven words: her comfort is her problem.
## The year on the docket
Then came the paperwork. None of the entries below is a conviction, and several ended with no charges at all. But read in a row, they make a pattern.

Accusations are not findings of guilt."}
A few of those deserve a closer look.
The alligator case came with a condition you don't see every day: prosecutors said he couldn't stream or make money from his community service. Even his punishment had to be kept off camera.

The April collapse happened live. A fellow creator, Androgenic, said they cut the stream and got him to a hospital. Afterward Peters said he'd been using substances to cope with being out in public, then added: "The worst part of tonight was my face descending from the life support mask." By July, on Sean Hannity's show, the story had changed: "I didn't overdose or anything," he said. Too much to drink, not enough to eat.

The Aqualyx claim is central to what's left of the Florida civil suit. The FDA lists Aqualyx among fat-dissolving injections it has never approved, and warns of serious infections, scarring and deformity, especially when unlicensed people do the injecting. The suit says Peters claimed he was qualified. He disputes the whole account.
## How he talks to people

In April, 60 Minutes Australia's Adam Hegarty asked him about Andrew Tate. Peters answered with a sexual insult about Hegarty's wife. Hegarty doesn't have one. Peters ended the interview. His spokesperson said he didn't want to talk politics.
That reflex says more than the forum jargon does. Ask him a hard question and he reaches for a woman, even an invented one, as a weapon.

In July, on a trip to Tel Aviv, an adviser to Benjamin Netanyahu, Topaz Luk, said Peters told him he regretted an antisemitic statement and planned to apologize publicly. Luk's response, reported by JTA: "We'll wait and see."
## The mainstream calls

None of this slowed the bookings. By September he was a guest on Howie Mandel's podcast, Red Scare and All In, The Bulwark reported, introduced as a fascinating new phenomenon. That tally comes from the same Bulwark story that broke the rape charges.
Nobody's saying hosts endorse every word a guest says. But a microphone is a choice, and most of this file was already public.
## The price of the face

Strip away the cheekbones and the pitch is simple: you're ugly, that's why you're lonely, and pain is the fix. Meth for hollow cheeks. Testosterone before 15. A hammer to the jaw. Research ties methamphetamine to heart rhythm problems and heart muscle disease, and ties steroid abuse to infertility and cardiovascular damage. That's what the drugs do in general. It doesn't diagnose Peters. It does describe what's being sold to the kids watching.

And the women in the picture get two jobs: proof that the method works, and content for the stream. The men in the audience don't do much better. Their loneliness is the product. He told the Times as much.
## What happens now
The Massachusetts case will be decided on evidence, in court. He is presumed innocent, and should be.

The question for everyone else doesn't need a verdict. A kid starts out at 14 wanting a different face so people will want him around. A man at 20 is selling that wish back to other kids, with a hammer, a needle and a theory about what women are for. You don't need a jury to decide whether to buy it.
